entries.title: How could Viking longships travel by sail or by oar?
entries.answer: Some Viking Age sailors used long, narrow boats moved by a sail or by oars. A crew could row if the wind did not help, and it could use the sail for longer trips in a favorable wind. The shallow hull let certain boats work close to land and enter smaller waterways. Other ships had wider bodies for carrying heavier goods. Archaeologists can study pieces of surviving ships to see how the wood and fittings once held the boat together.
facts: One small longship preserved in Denmark had room for a crew to row along both sides.

entries.title: How did cities change in Song China?
entries.answer: During the Song dynasty, people in Chinese cities bought goods from shops and markets and read books printed in growing numbers. Printing with carved blocks let a maker produce many pages from the same design. Shops, workshops, and travel also helped new ways of doing jobs reach more people. Meanwhile painters studied details such as trees and streams, or made pictures of busy city life. Art and records from the period show how closely merchants, craftspeople, and city families depended on one another.
facts: Northern Song rulers governed from Kaifeng before the dynasty’s court moved south.

entries.title: How did Haiti become an independent country?
entries.answer: France once ruled a colony in the western part of the island of Hispaniola, where many people were enslaved on plantations. In 1791, enslaved people began a large uprising. Fighting lasted for years and included groups with different goals. Toussaint Louverture helped lead forces that had fought to end slavery. After further conflict, Haitian leaders declared independence in 1804. The new country’s beginning showed that people who had lived through slavery could win freedom and build a state of their own.
facts: Toussaint Louverture died before Haiti declared independence.

entries.title: How did Nelson Mandela help change South Africa?
entries.answer: Nelson Mandela helped organize against apartheid, the system that denied many people equal rights in South Africa. He spent many years in prison. After his release, he took part in talks about ending apartheid and preparing a new election. In 1994, South Africa held its first fully democratic national election. Citizens of all races could vote, and Mandela became president. Many people did this work alongside him, and changing the law did not quickly solve every problem they faced.
facts: Nelson Mandela spent about 27 years in prison before his release in 1990.

entries.title: How did the Mongol Empire connect distant places?
entries.answer: Chinggis Khan united many groups on the grasslands of Inner Asia early in the thirteenth century. He and the rulers who followed him took control of lands far beyond those grasslands. For many communities the fighting brought harm. Under Mongol rule, some roads also carried more diplomats, craftspeople, travelers, and merchants moving among regions. As the empire grew, different branches of the ruling family governed different parts of it. One branch founded the Yuan dynasty in China.
facts: Chinggis Khan and Genghis Khan are different spellings of the same title.

entries.title: How did the Panama Canal change ocean travel?
entries.answer: Before the Panama Canal opened, ships traveling between the Atlantic and Pacific sides of the Americas often had to sail far around South America. Workers in Panama dug through hills, built dams, and made locks to raise ships to a lake and lower them again. The canal opened to traffic in 1914. The United States managed it for decades before agreements set a date for Panama to take over. Panama began managing the whole canal at the end of 1999.
facts: The official opening was marked by a passage of the ship Ancon in August 1914.

entries.title: How did towns of the Swahili coast trade across the ocean?
entries.answer: For centuries, merchants from towns along the eastern coast of Africa traded across the Indian Ocean. Sailors learned when winds were likely to carry boats toward Africa or away from it. Coastal traders sent some goods inland and received others, such as gold, from networks farther into Africa. Ships also brought goods such as pottery made across the ocean. Finds in coastal houses give clues about these trips. They show that the towns were part of a much wider trade network.
facts: Many trading towns along the coast were connected by the use of the Swahili language.

entries.title: How did trade help the Mali Empire grow?
entries.answer: The Mali Empire grew in West Africa along routes that linked regions with very different useful goods. Gold came from parts of West Africa, and salt could be brought from mines in the Sahara. Caravans carried loads between markets, and rulers gained power by protecting trade and collecting part of its value. Towns could grow as schools, religious buildings, and markets drew people in. Stories and written records make Mali especially well known during the rule of Mansa Musa.
facts: Mali grew into a major regional power from the thirteenth century onward.

entries.title: How did water shape the city of Angkor?
entries.answer: Angkor grew in a part of Southeast Asia where rain changes greatly between seasons. Khmer builders made channels and wide places that could hold water. They also set roads and temples within this large network. Archaeologists study old water routes to learn how farms and neighborhoods fit together, although experts still discuss just how different parts worked. Angkor covered much more land than the temples most visitors see. Its waterways and remains of settlement show what it took to support a large community.
facts: Angkor was home to a series of Khmer capitals in what is now Cambodia.

entries.title: What changed for Japan during the Meiji Restoration?
entries.answer: In 1868, Japan’s government changed after centuries during which military rulers called shoguns had held much of its power. A new government ruled in the name of the emperor, whose reign was called Meiji. Leaders changed the way regions were governed and studied ways of building schools, railways, and industry. People in different walks of life had to learn how to work with new rules and opportunities. Change was uneven, and many older ways of living continued alongside new ones.
facts: The city formerly called Edo became known as Tokyo near the start of the Meiji period.

entries.title: What did people do during the Viking Age?
entries.answer: During the Viking Age, people from parts of northern Europe traveled far by boat. Some raided towns, and others came to trade or settle. The same person or group might do different things on different trips. Many people stayed near home, where they farmed, cooked, repaired tools, and raised families. The things archaeologists find can show an ordinary day as well as an unusual journey. Coins and tools from different lands are clues that distant places were connected.
facts: The Viking Age is often dated from the late 700s to the middle or late 1000s in Europe.

entries.title: What do old buildings on an island in Tanzania reveal about trade?
entries.answer: Kilwa Kisiwani was a Swahili town on an island just off what is now Tanzania. Its people built homes, places of worship, and a palace using stone, including rock formed by coral. Among the ruins, archaeologists found pieces of pottery that had traveled from places far across the Indian Ocean. The pottery helps trace trade routes that no longer have the same stopovers. Looking at both the buildings and the small objects gives clues about how Kilwa became a busy and wealthy port.
facts: The ruins of another nearby Swahili town are on Songo Mnara.

entries.title: What happened on November 11, 1918?
entries.answer: By late 1918, the First World War had gone on for more than four years. Representatives of Germany and the countries fighting it agreed to an armistice, a promise to stop fighting under specific terms. It took effect at eleven in the morning on November 11 on the Western Front. The agreement came before the final peace treaties. Many places still observe the date today to remember people affected by the war and later wars.
facts: The agreement was signed in a railway carriage in France.

entries.title: What shows that Norse travelers reached North America?
entries.answer: At L’Anse aux Meadows on Newfoundland, archaeologists found traces of buildings and objects made by Norse travelers. Turf once covered parts of the structures, helping people live in a windy coastal place. Pieces from iron work and other activities show that visitors did jobs there as well as sleeping. This happened around a thousand years ago. Indigenous people already knew and used the region. The site gives us evidence of one early Atlantic crossing that we can study in detail.
facts: The site is on the northern tip of Newfoundland’s Great Northern Peninsula.

entries.title: What was apartheid in South Africa?
entries.answer: Apartheid was a system of laws in South Africa that separated people by race. It gave white people most political power and put limits on where many other people could live, travel, study, or work. South Africans opposed the system in many ways, and people in other countries added pressure. Over time, leaders agreed to end the laws and hold an election open to adult citizens of all races. That election in 1994 marked a big change.
facts: Laws enforcing apartheid were strengthened after the National Party came to power in 1948.

entries.title: Where did Zheng He’s fleets travel?
entries.answer: In the early 1400s, the rulers of Ming China sent fleets of ships across the Indian Ocean. A leader named Zheng He commanded several of these journeys. The ships stopped in ports in Southeast Asia, along India, and as far away as eastern Africa. Members of the fleets met rulers and carried gifts and goods. Rather than sailing into an empty sea, they traveled along routes where many groups already traded. The journeys show how far people and goods could move by ship.
facts: Zheng He is usually credited with leading seven voyages between 1405 and 1433.

entries.title: Why did Constantinople become an important city?
entries.answer: Constantinople stood beside the Bosporus, a narrow waterway connecting larger seas between Europe and Asia. That position brought ships and trade near the city. The Roman emperor Constantine made it an imperial capital in the fourth century. Even after Roman rule in western Europe changed, emperors continued to govern from Constantinople. Historians often call their state the Byzantine Empire. The city’s location helped it stay important under later rulers too, and it is now known as Istanbul.
facts: The Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople in 1453.

entries.title: Why did countries create the League of Nations?
entries.answer: After the First World War, leaders wanted countries to have a place to talk through disagreements before turning to fighting. The League of Nations began in 1920, with its center in Geneva, Switzerland. Countries sent representatives to meetings and tried to cooperate on difficult problems. Some important countries did not join or left over time. The League could not stop the Second World War. Its work and problems helped leaders think about how to build another organization after that war.
facts: The United States never joined the League, even though a US president had helped propose it.

entries.title: Why did countries form the United Nations?
entries.answer: Near the end of the Second World War, delegates from many countries came to San Francisco. They wrote a charter for an organization called the United Nations. They wanted countries to talk about conflicts, work together on problems, and support equal rights. Member countries can still disagree, so meetings and rules do not make every problem easy to solve. The United Nations gives countries a shared place to discuss some problems affecting more than one country.
facts: The United Nations Charter went into effect on October 24, 1945.

entries.title: Why did Mansa Musa travel across Africa?
entries.answer: Mansa Musa was a ruler of the Mali Empire. In the 1300s he went on pilgrimage to Mecca, a city important to Muslims. His group crossed the Sahara and spent time in Cairo. Stories about the visit describe how gifts and spending revealed the wealth of Mali to people far from the empire. Accounts of the trip traveled far, and a mapmaker in Europe later pictured Mansa Musa holding gold.
facts: The Catalan Atlas, a map made in the late 1300s, shows Mansa Musa holding a piece of gold.

entries.title: Why did more people begin working in factories?
entries.answer: For a long time, people could spin thread or weave cloth in homes and small workshops. In Britain, larger machines made it possible to gather several parts of this work in one place. Water or steam could power machines in a mill, and many workers could work under the same roof. Cloth could be made more quickly, but workers had to keep to the machines’ pace and often worked long days. Changes like these also helped industrial cities grow.
facts: Cotton mills helped Manchester grow into a large industrial city.

entries.title: Why did people dig a canal across part of Egypt?
entries.answer: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea through Egypt. A ship traveling between parts of Europe and Asia can use it rather than going all the way around southern Africa. Workers had to cut a long channel across fairly low desert land and through some lakes. The canal opened to shipping in 1869. Many ships that once made the longer trip around Africa could then follow a shorter route through Egypt.
facts: The Suez Canal has no locks because ships move along a channel at sea level.

entries.title: Why did Timbuktu become a center for books?
entries.answer: Timbuktu grew near a point where desert travelers could connect with routes into West Africa. Markets brought people to the town, and scholars came to teach and study. Students might work with lessons about law, faith, language, or other subjects. People copied books by hand and kept them in family or school collections. Timbuktu is especially known for its mosques and earthen buildings. They are part of a living city, where people still care for buildings and older writings.
facts: Timbuktu is in present-day Mali, south of the Sahara Desert.

entries.title: Why did travelers come to the Tang capital?
entries.answer: During the Tang dynasty, Chang’an was a large capital with ordered streets and busy markets. Officials, traders, and travelers arrived from far apart places. Some foreign goods entered the city through trade routes across Asia. Artists pictured traveling musicians, horses, and merchants in objects that survive today. Goods moved outward too. Looking at the different people and things shown in Tang art helps us see a city where cultures kept meeting as people traded and traveled.
facts: Chang’an stood near modern Xi’an, a city in central China.

entries.title: Why do people call many routes the Silk Roads?
entries.answer: The Silk Roads were linked routes between parts of Asia and places farther west. Travelers could choose different roads depending on the season, water, or who controlled a pass. A merchant often took a load only as far as the next town or market. Another person might carry it on from there. Silk was one famous trade good, but travelers also brought new ideas, stories, foods, and ways of making things. Exchange could continue even when particular routes became hard to use.
facts: Some of the routes crossed deserts and high mountains, where travelers needed stopping places with water.

entries.title: Why was Berlin once divided by a wall?
entries.answer: After the Second World War, Germany and the city of Berlin were split into areas controlled by different governments. In 1961, East German leaders built a barrier through and around West Berlin to stop people from leaving across the city’s border. The wall split streets and made it hard for neighbors and families to visit. In 1989 crowds gathered at border crossings after officials announced a change, and guards began letting people through. Germany reunited the following year.
facts: The border crossings opened on the night of November 9, 1989.
